title: Day 1 · Phase 1 — Re-anchoring: heat is energy, but it's not temperature
bodyHtml:
DAY 1 · Phase 1 — Setting up the question

Unit 4 said "energy lost to friction becomes heat." Unit 5 quantifies the heat — and untangles heat from temperature.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS (preview)

K1. Distinguish thermal energy, temperature, and heat. R3. Why atmospheric entry GLOWS — preview to Day 10.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have estimated the fictional asteroid’s kinetic energy. This unit follows energy transfers during entry and impact and distinguishes temperature, thermal energy, and heat.

How today connects:

end of Unit 4. We have impact KE in TNT equivalents. The damage isn't just shockwave — it's HEAT.

Today's pivot: Two payoffs in Unit 5. (1) atmospheric entry — Day 10 explains why most asteroids burn up before they hit. (2) impact thermal damage — Day 11 explains the fireball and thermal radiation that does damage even outside the crater zone.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Return Unit 4 transfer tasks. Highlight strong yield-conversion work. "Energy was the damage answer. But the damage MECHANISM is heat. Today we untangle heat from temperature."

5–18 min

Comparison: Use labeled diagrams of 0.005 kg liquid water at 100 °C and 100 kg at 40 °C. With liquid water at 0 °C as the common reference, compare mass × temperature rise. The larger sample has greater energy increase; the smaller one has higher temperature. Discuss initial heat-flow direction.

18–28 min

Temperature determines spontaneous heat-flow direction. In the ideal-gas model it is proportional to average translational kinetic energy. Internal energy includes microscopic kinetic and interaction potential energy; liquid water needs the broader model. Heat is energy transferred because of temperature difference.

28–42 min

• Mini-lecture preview: Unit 5's three big landings. (1) calorimetry lab Day 5. (2) entropy + heat-engine efficiency on Days 8–9 (why perpetual motion machines fail). (3) atmospheric entry + impact heat on Days 10–11 — the asteroid payoff.

42–48 min

• Individual exit: Compare 0.005 kg of liquid water at 100 °C with 100 kg of liquid water at 40 °C, using liquid water at 0 °C as the common reference and the same specific heat. Which has higher temperature? Which has the larger internal-energy increase? If they exchange energy directly, which way does heat initially flow? Explain using amount and temperature.

48–50 min

• Marzano on K1 preview.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Look for a distinction between temperature and internal-energy change with a common reference. Heat flows initially from higher to lower temperature, regardless of which sample has more mass.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: Unit 4 transfer tasks scored; thermometer for prop; cup + a comparison image of a bathtub; match prop (don't light) or video.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 21 §21.1. Honors: Ch 21 §21.1–21.4.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §13.1 Temperature (pp. 566–569); §14.1 Heat (pp. 618–620). Focus: Distinguish temperature, internal energy, and heat as energy transfer; compare particle-scale and macroscopic descriptions. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on temperature vs. thermal energy: when students conflate them, push: "If I have two glasses at the same temperature but one twice as much water — same thermal energy or different? Why?"

Differentiation: ELs — three-column glossary (heat / temperatura / calor — each defined visually); SWDs — verbal version of exit ticket offered; Honors extension — "if I combined the hot coffee with the cold lake (no other losses), what final temperature?"

Scientific distinction: Chelyabinsk’s windows were broken by the shock wave. Thermal radiation and blast are separate pathways. Internal energy includes microscopic kinetic and potential contributions; do not apply an ideal-gas-only definition to liquid water.

CPA teaching sequence: Use a picture of the system and an energy-flow arrow before an equation. Supply a table of masses, temperature changes, and constants; model each warming or phase-change stage separately before combining them.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 2 · Phase 2 — Specific heat: Q = mcΔT
bodyHtml:
DAY 2 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Different materials need different amounts of energy per kg per °C. Water is the outlier (huge c).

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K2. Specific heat. S1. Compute Q = mcΔT.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have estimated the fictional asteroid’s kinetic energy. This unit follows energy transfers during entry and impact and distinguishes temperature, thermal energy, and heat. The preceding meeting focused on Re-anchoring: heat is energy, but it's not temperature.

How today connects:

Asteroids are mostly rock (c ≈ 800 J/kg·°C). Oceans are water (c ≈ 4186). When 2026-XJ heats up during atmospheric entry, the SAME energy raises rock temperature 5× more than it would water.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hand back exit tickets. Anchor: "Heat and temperature are connected by a constant called specific heat."

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: Q = m·c·ΔT. Q = heat (J). m = mass (kg). c = specific heat (J/kg·°C). ΔT = temperature change (°C). Walk through each piece. Show the specific heat table — water c = 4186, aluminum 900, copper 387, ice 2090, rock 800.

18–32 min

• Worked example sequence: (1) How much heat to raise 0.5 kg of water by 20 °C? (2) Same energy applied to 0.5 kg of aluminum — what's the temperature rise? Force the room to see WHY water heats slowly.

32–42 min

• Group practice — 5 problems mixing materials, masses, and ΔT. Include one where the unknown is c (so they solve for material identification).

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "How much heat is needed to raise 2 kg of copper from 20 °C to 80 °C?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K2/S1.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check mass units and temperature change, not absolute temperature, in Q = mcΔT. Students should explain why equal energy transfers need not cause equal temperature changes.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: specific-heat table printed; packet practice; calculator availability.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 21 §21.6. Honors: Ch 21 §21.5–21.7 + Think and Solve 54, 57, 61.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §14.2 Temperature Change and Heat Capacity (pp. 620–625). Focus: Use mass, specific heat, and temperature change to model energy transfer; keep temperature difference separate from absolute temperature. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on water's anomaly: push: "Water has c that's ~5× rock and ~10× metals. Why does it take so long to heat a pot of water? And why are oceans the planet's thermostat?"

Differentiation: ELs — equation with each piece labeled in words; SWDs — pre-built table for the worked examples; Honors extension — "if you heat 100 g of aluminum and 100 g of copper with the same 500 J, which gets hotter?"

CPA teaching sequence: Use a picture of the system and an energy-flow arrow before an equation. Supply a table of masses, temperature changes, and constants; model each warming or phase-change stage separately before combining them.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 3 · Phase 2 — Heat transfer: conduction, convection, radiation
bodyHtml:
DAY 3 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Conduction — touch. Convection — fluid currents. Radiation — light.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K3. Distinguish the three heat-transfer modes. Identify each in real scenarios.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have estimated the fictional asteroid’s kinetic energy. This unit follows energy transfers during entry and impact and distinguishes temperature, thermal energy, and heat. The preceding meeting focused on Specific heat: Q = mcΔT.

How today connects:

Atmospheric entry heat moves THREE ways: friction (conduction at the asteroid surface), convection (heated air swept around it), and radiation (the asteroid GLOWS — and energy escapes as light). All three lose energy from the asteroid.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hook: "Hot soup. How does it cool down?" Get students to name multiple paths.

5–22 min

• Direct instruction with demos. Conduction: hold a metal spoon in hot water — the handle warms (direct molecular contact). Convection: watch dye in a heated beaker — rises with the warmer (less dense) fluid. Radiation: hold hand near a hot mug WITHOUT TOUCHING — you feel infrared heat at distance (no medium needed).

22–35 min

• Classify activity: 8 real-world heat scenarios on a worksheet. Sun warming Earth. Hot drink in your hand. Convection oven. Wind chill. Asteroid glowing during entry. Microwave. House insulation. Pair-share answers.

35–43 min

• Class compilation: name each scenario by mode. Discuss disagreements.

43–48 min

• Exit ticket: "You see a glowing meteor cross the sky. By which mode does the meteor lose energy to YOU on the ground?" (Radiation only — vacuum/air between.)

48–50 min

• Marzano on K3.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Ask students to identify what moves in conduction, convection, and radiation. Radiation does not require material between the source and receiver.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: spoon + hot water beaker; food-color dye + warm-water beaker for convection; hot mug; classify-the-scenario worksheet.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 22 §22.1. Honors: Ch 22 §22.1–22.5 + Think and Solve 40, 43.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §14.4 Heat Transfer Methods (pp. 632–633); §14.5 Conduction (pp. 633–635); §14.6 Convection (pp. 639–641); §14.7 Radiation (pp. 644–647). Focus: Compare conduction, convection, and radiation using the named introductory excerpts; detailed transfer-rate calculations are not assigned here. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on radiation vs. conduction: when students conflate them, push: "Does the mug touch your hand for radiation to work? What does that tell you?"

Differentiation: ELs — three-card visual (conduction / convection / radiation) with one example each; SWDs — fewer scenarios, more partner time; Honors extension — "why does a thermos use a vacuum gap? What modes does that defeat?"

CPA teaching sequence: Use a picture of the system and an energy-flow arrow before an equation. Supply a table of masses, temperature changes, and constants; model each warming or phase-change stage separately before combining them.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

title: Day 4 · Phase 2 — Phase changes + latent heat
bodyHtml:
DAY 4 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Q = mL. Phase changes happen at constant T while energy goes into breaking bonds.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K4. Phase changes + latent heat. S2. Compute Q = mL.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have estimated the fictional asteroid’s kinetic energy. This unit follows energy transfers during entry and impact and distinguishes temperature, thermal energy, and heat. The preceding meeting focused on Heat transfer: conduction, convection, radiation.

How today connects:

2026-XJ doesn't just heat up at impact — it MELTS, then VAPORIZES. Each transition takes enormous energy. The crater's heat doesn't just raise rock temperature, it phases rock into vapor.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hook: "Put a thermometer in a pot of boiling water. What temperature reads? It keeps boiling for 10 more minutes — does the temperature change?" (No — 100 °C.) Where does the heat go?

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: phase changes happen at constant T. Energy goes into breaking molecular bonds, not raising temperature. Latent heat L = energy per kg to phase-change. L_fusion (melt/freeze). L_vaporization (boil/condense). Water: L_f = 334 kJ/kg, L_v = 2260 kJ/kg.

18–30 min

• Worked example: how much heat to (a) raise 0.5 kg of ice from -20 °C to 0 °C — Q = mcΔT with c_ice. (b) MELT all that ice at 0 °C — Q = mL_f. (c) Raise water from 0 °C to 100 °C — Q = mcΔT with c_water. (d) BOIL all the water at 100 °C — Q = mL_v. Add them up — the latent steps DOMINATE.

30–42 min

• Plot temperature vs. heat for water — flat segments at the phase changes, sloped between. Show the canonical "heating curve."

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "How much heat to vaporize 0.2 kg of water at 100 °C?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K4/S2.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check separate warming and phase-change stages. During an ideal phase change at fixed pressure, energy can transfer without a temperature increase.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: Latent-heat table (water + a few others); heating-curve diagram for the board; packet practice.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 23 §23.8. Honors: Ch 23 §23.1, 23.2, 23.3, 23.4, 23.8 + Think and Solve 57, 58, 61.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §14.3 Phase Change and Latent Heat (pp. 626–632). Focus: Explain latent heat and constant temperature during a phase change; distinguish phase change from warming within one phase. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on the latent-heat scale: when students see L_v = 2260 kJ/kg for water, push: "Compare to raising water 80 °C: only 334 kJ/kg. Boiling is more energy-intensive than ALL the heating. Why does sweating cool you?"

Differentiation: ELs — heating-curve diagram with each segment labeled in words; SWDs — multi-step worksheet with each Q calculation pre-numbered; Honors extension — "compute the total heat to convert 1 kg of ice at -10 °C to steam at 110 °C."

CPA teaching sequence: Use a picture of the system and an energy-flow arrow before an equation. Supply a table of masses, temperature changes, and constants; model each warming or phase-change stage separately before combining them.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 5 · Phase 2 — Vernier calorimetry lab
bodyHtml:
DAY 5 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Mix water at two temperatures. Predict final temperature using Q_lost = Q_gained. Then measure with Vernier temp probe.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

S4. Vernier calorimetry. K2. Confirm specific-heat math.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have estimated the fictional asteroid’s kinetic energy. This unit follows energy transfers during entry and impact and distinguishes temperature, thermal energy, and heat. The preceding meeting focused on Phase changes + latent heat.

How today connects:

If we confirm Q = mcΔT works in our lab cups, we can use it on planetary scales for the impact heat calculations on Day 11.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Lab procedure overview + safety beat (hot water, gloves, careful pouring).

5–15 min

• Teacher demo: 100 mL water at 70 °C mixed with 100 mL at 20 °C. Predict T_final using m_h·c·(T_h - T_f) = m_c·c·(T_f - T_c). Then measure with probe.

15–35 min

• Lab: pairs run 3 trials varying masses + temperatures. Predict T_f, measure with Vernier temp probe, compute % difference. Then: drop a hot metal piece into cold water, use Q_metal = -Q_water to compute the metal's specific heat (identifies unknown material).

35–40 min

• Class data: average specific heat for the unknown metal. Compare to known c values, identify material.

40–43 min

Individual exit: Explain one result from today using a labeled sketch, calculation, or specific observation. State the model or relationship you used and one assumption. Use your own evidence before comparing with a partner.

43–48 min

• Lab write-up start.

48–50 min

• Marzano on S4.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Inspect measured masses and temperatures, the energy balance, and heat exchanged with the apparatus. A simple average is justified only for equal heat capacities in the ideal model.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: Vernier temperature probes + LabQuest; styrofoam cups (insulated calorimeters); hot plate + beakers of hot water; ice; balance; known metal pieces (aluminum + copper) labeled "unknown A / unknown B"; lab write-up template.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: no reading.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §14.2 Temperature Change and Heat Capacity (pp. 620–625). Focus: Set up energy gained and lost in the calorimetry system and identify heat exchange with the surroundings as a source of discrepancy. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on % difference: if a pair is 5% off, push: "What ENERGY is leaking out of your calorimeter? Where would it go?"

Differentiation: ELs — pair with a partner familiar with LoggerPro; SWDs — pre-built data table; Honors extension — "compute the heat lost to the cup itself using the cup's mass and specific heat. Does that close the gap?"

CPA teaching sequence: Use a picture of the system and an energy-flow arrow before an equation. Supply a table of masses, temperature changes, and constants; model each warming or phase-change stage separately before combining them.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

title: Day 6 · Phase 2 — Kinetic theory: temperature is molecular KE
bodyHtml:
DAY 6 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Temperature ∝ average kinetic energy of molecules. Higher T = faster jiggling.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

Use the classical ideal-gas model: mean translational kinetic energy per particle is (3/2)kT. For the same gas species, rms speed grows as √T. Internal energy of real matter also includes microscopic interaction, rotational and vibrational contributions.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have estimated the fictional asteroid’s kinetic energy. This unit follows energy transfers during entry and impact and distinguishes temperature, thermal energy, and heat. The preceding meeting focused on Vernier calorimetry lab.

How today connects:

When the asteroid impact vaporizes rock, what's happening at the molecular level? Molecules gain enough KE to break free from solid → liquid → gas. Kinetic theory connects the energy framework to the molecular picture.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hook: "You added energy yesterday and got a temperature change. Where did that energy GO inside the water?"

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: kinetic theory of gases. Molecules jiggle randomly. Temperature is proportional to the AVERAGE KE per molecule: KE_avg = (3/2)kT (k = Boltzmann constant). Higher T → faster avg molecular speed.

18–30 min

• Phase change as bond-breaking: in a solid, molecules vibrate in place. As T rises, KE grows. At melting point, KE is enough to break bonds → liquid. At boiling, even more → gas. The LATENT heat from Day 4 goes into bond-breaking, not avg KE.

30–40 min

• PhET States of Matter sim: heat solid argon. Watch molecular motion increase. See phase transitions.

40–48 min

• Exit ticket: "Why does temperature stay constant during a phase change, even though heat is being added?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K1 extended.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check use of kelvin in kinetic-theory comparisons. For a fixed ideal-gas species, doubling absolute temperature doubles mean translational KE and increases rms speed by the square root of two.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: PhET States of Matter loaded on lab computers; molecular-motion visualization for the board.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 21 §21.1. Honors: Ch 21 §21.1 + Think and Solve 62, 63; Ch 24 §24.1.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §13.4 Kinetic Theory: Atomic and Molecular Explanation of Pressure and Temperature (pp. 589–595). Focus: Connect molecular motion with pressure and temperature; use absolute temperature in the kinetic model. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on the constant-T-during-phase-change explanation: push: "Where is the heat going if not into avg KE? What's it doing to the molecules?" Lead to bond-breaking.

Differentiation: ELs — visual showing molecular vibration intensity vs. T; SWDs — fill-in answer template for exit ticket; Honors extension — "if T doubles (Kelvin), what happens to avg molecular speed? Hint: KE = ½mv²."

Model boundary

Use T = °C + 273.15. Temperature is not mean speed. The ideal-gas translational-energy relation does not define all the internal energy of liquid water. For the same gas species, rms speed scales as √T; phase changes can change interaction potential energy at constant temperature.

CPA teaching sequence: Use a picture of the system and an energy-flow arrow before an equation. Supply a table of masses, temperature changes, and constants; model each warming or phase-change stage separately before combining them.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

title: Day 7 · Phase 2 — First law of thermodynamics: ΔU = Q − W
bodyHtml:
DAY 7 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Change in internal energy = heat in MINUS work out. Energy conservation, written for gases.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K5. First law of thermodynamics.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have estimated the fictional asteroid’s kinetic energy. This unit follows energy transfers during entry and impact and distinguishes temperature, thermal energy, and heat. The preceding meeting focused on Kinetic theory: temperature is molecular KE.

How today connects:

The expanding fireball after impact is a thermodynamic system — gas at high T expanding against the surrounding atmosphere. The first law describes how its thermal energy converts to work pushing on the air (shockwave).

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Recap: energy conservation (Unit 4). Heat is a form of energy (Day 1).

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: ΔU = Q − W. ΔU = change in internal energy (thermal energy of the system). Q = heat ADDED to the system. W = work DONE BY the system on surroundings. The minus sign matters.

18–30 min

• Worked example 1: 500 J heat added to a gas. The gas does 200 J of work expanding. ΔU = 500 − 200 = 300 J. Internal energy rises.

30–40 min

• Worked example 2: a gas is compressed — 300 J of work is done ON it. No heat exchanged (adiabatic). W = -300 (gas did negative work). ΔU = 0 − (-300) = 300 J. Compression HEATS the gas. (This is why a bike pump gets warm.)

40–48 min

• Exit ticket: "100 J heat enters a system. The system does 150 J of work. What's ΔU?" (-50 J — internal energy DECREASES.)

48–50 min

• Marzano on K5.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check the declared sign convention: Q into the system and W done by the system in ΔU = Q − W. Students must identify the system before substituting signs.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: bike pump for compression demo; packet practice; sign-convention chart (Q positive = heat in; W positive = work BY system).

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 24 §24.2. Honors: Ch 24 §24.1–24.3 + Think and Solve 50.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §15.1 The First Law of Thermodynamics (pp. 665–669). Focus: Use the book's first-law sign convention and identify heat into the system and work done by the system. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on the sign convention: students will mix up signs. Stop on every problem: "Is heat going IN or OUT? Is work being done BY or ON the system?"

Differentiation: ELs — sign-chart card; SWDs — pre-filled Q and W signs on worksheet; Honors extension — "how does the first law apply to a refrigerator? What's the sign of Q?"

CPA teaching sequence: Use a picture of the system and an energy-flow arrow before an equation. Supply a table of masses, temperature changes, and constants; model each warming or phase-change stage separately before combining them.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

title: Day 8 · Phase 2 — Second law: heat flows hot → cold; entropy
bodyHtml:
DAY 8 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Heat NEVER spontaneously flows cold to hot. Entropy of the universe always increases.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K6. Second law of thermodynamics + entropy direction. R1. Reason about which processes are spontaneous.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have estimated the fictional asteroid’s kinetic energy. This unit follows energy transfers during entry and impact and distinguishes temperature, thermal energy, and heat. The preceding meeting focused on First law of thermodynamics: ΔU = Q − W.

How today connects:

The asteroid's KE at impact becomes thermal energy — that's a HIGH-entropy state. There's no natural process that converts the heat back to organized motion. The impact is IRREVERSIBLE in this sense.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hook: "Have you ever seen a broken glass un-shatter? Have you ever seen heat spontaneously flow from cold to hot? Why not?"

5–20 min

• Direct instruction: Second law (Clausius form): heat flows naturally from HOT to COLD, never the reverse, without external work. Entropy is a measure of disorder. Spontaneous processes increase entropy of the universe.

20–32 min

• Examples: melting ice (water has higher entropy than ice — molecules can move more). Diffusion of gas. Mixing hot + cold water (entropy higher than separated). The arrow of time is the arrow of entropy.

32–42 min

• Group discussion: classify 6 scenarios as entropy-INCREASING (spontaneous) or entropy-decreasing (requires energy input). Egg breaking. Refrigerator cooling food. Sun warming Earth. Battery being charged. Iron rusting. Water freezing in a freezer.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "Why can't you cool your kitchen by leaving the refrigerator door open?" (Because the heat dumped to the back of the fridge exceeds the heat removed from inside — net heating.)

48–50 min

• Marzano on K6/R1.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Look for heat flowing spontaneously hot to cold and total entropy of system plus surroundings. Local ordering alone does not disprove the second law.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: packet practice; entropy classification worksheet.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 24 §24.4. Honors: Ch 24 §24.4, 24.6, 24.7 + Think and Solve 43, 44.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §15.3 Introduction to the Second Law of Thermodynamics: Heat Engines and Their Efficiency (pp. 678–680); §15.6 Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics: Disorder and the Unavailability of Energy (pp. 694–697). Focus: Describe one-way energy transfers and entropy change for the system plus surroundings; avoid equating entropy only with visible messiness. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on "fridge with door open": when students reach for "it would cool," push: "Where does the heat removed from inside the fridge GO? Compare to the cooling effect on the room."

Differentiation: ELs — "hot → cold" visual arrows; SWDs — partner discussion on each scenario; Honors extension — "could a perpetual motion machine exist that doesn't violate the FIRST law but does violate the SECOND? Why does the second law forbid it?"

CPA teaching sequence: Use a picture of the system and an energy-flow arrow before an equation. Supply a table of masses, temperature changes, and constants; model each warming or phase-change stage separately before combining them.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 9 · Phase 2 — Heat engines + efficiency
bodyHtml:
DAY 9 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Engines take heat from hot source, do work, dump waste heat to cold sink. Efficiency = W/Q_hot.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K7. Heat engine cycle + efficiency. S3. Compute efficiency.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have estimated the fictional asteroid’s kinetic energy. This unit follows energy transfers during entry and impact and distinguishes temperature, thermal energy, and heat. The preceding meeting focused on Second law: heat flows hot → cold; entropy.

How today connects:

The expanding fireball after impact is a NATURAL heat engine — it converts some of its thermal energy to mechanical work (the shockwave). But it can't convert 100% — the second law forbids it.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Quick check: second law direction.

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: heat engines move heat from HOT to COLD and extract some as WORK along the way. Efficiency = W/Q_hot = 1 − Q_cold/Q_hot. Always < 1. The second law forces SOME heat to be wasted.

18–32 min

• Worked examples: a power plant gets 1000 J from steam at 600 K, does 400 J of work, dumps 600 J to cold sink at 300 K. Efficiency = 40%. Compare to ideal Carnot efficiency: 1 − T_cold/T_hot = 1 − 300/600 = 50%. Real engines are less efficient than the Carnot LIMIT.

32–42 min

• Group practice — 4 problems. Compute real and Carnot efficiencies. Compare typical engines: car (~25%), power plant (~40%), human body (~25%).

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A car engine receives 1500 J of heat per cycle and produces 400 J of work. What's its efficiency?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K7/S3.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check work output as heat in minus heat out and efficiency as work divided by heat in. Carnot temperatures must be absolute temperatures in kelvin.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: packet practice; engine efficiency reference chart; calculator availability.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 24 §24.5. Honors: Ch 24 §24.5 + Think and Solve 51, 55, 57.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §15.3 Introduction to the Second Law of Thermodynamics: Heat Engines and Their Efficiency (pp. 680–684); §15.4 Carnot’s Perfect Heat Engine: The Second Law of Thermodynamics Restated (pp. 685–689). Focus: Read engine energy-flow diagrams and compare actual efficiency with an ideal limit; use kelvin where required. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on the Carnot LIMIT: push: "This is the MOST efficient engine that could possibly exist between these temperatures. Real engines are below this. Why is the limit set by temperatures alone?"

Differentiation: ELs — efficiency equation card with each piece labeled; SWDs — pre-built worksheet (Q_hot, W, Q_cold columns); Honors extension — "derive Carnot efficiency from second law principles."

CPA teaching sequence: Use a picture of the system and an energy-flow arrow before an equation. Supply a table of masses, temperature changes, and constants; model each warming or phase-change stage separately before combining them.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 10 · Phase 2 — Atmospheric entry: why most asteroids burn up
bodyHtml:
DAY 10 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Most space rocks NEVER reach the ground. Atmosphere does negative work, all of it becomes heat.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

R3. Reason about atmospheric entry thermodynamics.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have estimated the fictional asteroid’s kinetic energy. This unit follows energy transfers during entry and impact and distinguishes temperature, thermal energy, and heat. The preceding meeting focused on Heat engines + efficiency.

How today connects:

If 2026-XJ is small enough, ALL its KE goes into atmospheric heating before it touches the ground. If it's big enough to survive, only PART burns away. Today: what's the size threshold?

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hook: a shooting star. What you're seeing is a sand-grain-to-pebble-sized rock burning up. Most of its mass becomes vapor before it reaches the ground.

5–18 min

• Mini-lecture: atmospheric drag is a friction-like force. At 15 km/s, drag is ENORMOUS. The work done by drag = ½ρ·v²·A·d. All of that becomes thermal energy at the surface of the rock.

18–32 min

• Worked example: a 1-kg pebble at 15 km/s. Its KE = ½·1·(15000)² = 1.1×10⁸ J. To vaporize all 1 kg of rock requires ~10⁷ J (using rock c + L_v). So all its KE × about 10 is available — the pebble TOTALLY vaporizes. Now repeat for a 10-kg rock — most still vaporizes but some core may survive. For 1000 kg, maybe 10% mass loss. For 10⁹ kg (like 2026-XJ), atmospheric losses are negligible — it reaches ground at nearly full mass.

32–42 min

• Class discussion: why does this matter for planetary defense? Small rocks are atmospheric problem (Chelyabinsk: airburst at 30 km, no crater, glass-shattering shockwave but no impact). Big rocks are ground problem.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "Why does a 1-kg rock burn up but a 10⁹-kg asteroid reach the ground? Reason in terms of surface area to mass ratio."

48–50 min

• Marzano on R3.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Require students to state the fraction of incoming kinetic energy assumed to heat the object. Energy availability alone does not establish survival; size, entry conditions, and energy transfer matter.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: Chelyabinsk 2013 video or photo (the dashcam reels are iconic); atmospheric density reference; calculator.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: Ch 22 §22.4–22.5 + Think and Solve 44.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §5.2 Drag Forces (pp. 219–223); §14.3 Phase Change and Latent Heat (pp. 626–632). Focus: Use drag and phase-change ideas to organize the atmospheric-entry model. Use the course sources for compression, ablation, and atmospheric details. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on the size threshold: push: "Surface-area-to-mass scales as 1/r. Small rocks have lots of surface area per unit mass — lots of drag per unit of KE. Big rocks have little. Why is THIS the deciding factor?"

Differentiation: ELs — visual showing different-sized rocks with different drag-to-mass ratios; SWDs — pre-built KE-vs-vaporization-energy worksheet for 4 sizes; Honors extension — "what's the largest rock that completely burns up in our atmosphere? Estimate."

CPA teaching sequence: Use a picture of the system and an energy-flow arrow before an equation. Supply a table of masses, temperature changes, and constants; model each warming or phase-change stage separately before combining them.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 11 · Phase 2 — Asteroid impact thermal effects
bodyHtml:
DAY 11 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Model energy transfer after impact. Compare energy per area at different distances and identify the limits of an idealized model.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

R3. Apply thermal framework to predict impact damage modes.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have estimated the fictional asteroid’s kinetic energy. This unit follows energy transfers during entry and impact and distinguishes temperature, thermal energy, and heat. The preceding meeting focused on Atmospheric entry: why most asteroids burn up.

How today connects:

Use the impact-energy estimate from Unit 4 to follow possible transfers to heating and phase changes, mechanical motion, sound, and radiation. The partition depends on the impact conditions; this lesson uses explicitly assumed fractions for a sensitivity study.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Frame the day. "We have the impact KE in TNT. Today we trace where that energy goes thermally."

5–18 min

Group calculation: choose and label illustrative fractions for heating/phase change, mechanical motion, and radiation that sum to one. They are classroom assumptions, not measured percentages for 2026-XJ. Compute the energy in each branch and vary one fraction while keeping the total energy fixed.

18–32 min

Idealized spreading model: for an isotropic point source, calculate energy per area E_radiated/(4πr²) at three supplied distances. State the assumptions of equal spreading and no absorption or shielding. Compare the result when distance doubles; do not turn it into an injury or ignition radius.

32–42 min

Compilation: build an energy-per-area versus distance table. Label the assumed source energy and geometry. Identify additional information needed for a physical impact model: entry and breakup, surface geometry, duration, atmospheric transfer, and material response.

42–45 min

Discussion: which results follow from energy conservation and which depend on assumptions? Explain why a fast-traveling signal does not, by itself, establish the extent of damage.

45–48 min

Individual exit: Explain one result from today using a labeled sketch, calculation, or specific observation. State the model or relationship you used and one assumption. Use your own evidence before comparing with a partner.

48–50 min

• Marzano on R3.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check that assumed energy fractions and idealized spreading are labeled as model inputs. Students should explain why this classroom energy model cannot establish a real injury or damage radius.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: 2026-XJ KE from Unit 4 Day 19; thermal damage threshold reference; calculator; whiteboard space for damage map.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: Ch 22 §22.6–22.7.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §14.2 Temperature Change and Heat Capacity (pp. 620–625); §14.7 Radiation (pp. 644–648). Focus: Connect assumed energy partitions with heating and radiation. These models alone do not determine an injury or damage radius. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on partitioning: push: "How would you EXPERIMENTALLY measure which fraction goes where? Could you find that from a real crater?"

Differentiation: ELs — labeled energy-flow arrows and a distance table; SWDs — a worked example using separate practice values; Honors extension — compare two assumed radiation fractions and quantify the sensitivity without claiming a real damage forecast.

CPA teaching sequence: Use a picture of the system and an energy-flow arrow before an equation. Supply a table of masses, temperature changes, and constants; model each warming or phase-change stage separately before combining them.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

Teacher reference: NASA Asteroid Threat Assessment Project describes entry, breakup, blast, thermal, and tsunami modeling. Use it to distinguish the classroom model from a hazard forecast.

title: Day 12 · Phase 3 — Unit 5 transfer task, day 1: receive, plan, begin
bodyHtml:
DAY 12 · Phase 3 — Transfer task

Unit 5 Transfer Task Day 1: Receive, Plan, Begin

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

All Unit 5 targets, surfaced through transfer problems.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Use the evidence and supplied scenario data developed through this unit. Any new numerical data appear in the task itself; the asteroid remains fictional.

How today connects: Write a public-facing explanation of where energy can go during entry and impact. State what the model can and cannot tell us about the survival of 2026-XJ.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

Set the assessment conditions: individual work; calculator and the agreed equation/constants card allowed. Clarifying questions are welcome; physics-content coaching and new video help wait until after the assessment.

5–15 min

Read the task silently. Record what you notice and wonder. Clarify the meaning of the prompt and supplied data without discussing a solution.

15–25 min

Plan the work against Science / Reasoning / Communication / Transfer-to-Asteroid. Identify the needed diagrams, equations, evidence, units, assumptions, and public-facing explanation.

25–45 min

Begin the task independently. The teacher records approaches and access needs without giving content help.

45–50 min

Record the next step and the dimension that needs attention. Hand in work in progress for safekeeping; retrieve it at the next meeting. The task stays in class.

TRANSFER TASK

• Transfer task. Independent. 4 multi-part problems: (1) calorimetry — mix two known water samples + verify final temperature; (2) phase change — total heat to convert ice at -10 °C to steam at 110 °C; (3) heat engine — given Q_hot, Q_cold, compute W and efficiency, compare to Carnot; (4) asteroid atmospheric entry — given a pebble's mass + speed + needed vaporization energy, does it reach the ground?

Public-facing transfer: Write a public-facing explanation of where energy can go during entry and impact. State what the model can and cannot tell us about the survival of 2026-XJ.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check the individual plan for energy balances, stage boundaries, stated assumptions, and each rubric dimension. Provide task clarifications without supplying thermal reasoning.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: transfer task printed; calculators; constants reference card (c, L, k); quiet testing environment; growth chart pages.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: no reading.

Transfer task with all numerical data and assumptions; Unit 1 four-dimension rubric; permitted equation/constants card and calculator; planning sheet; a secure place to keep work between meetings.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: No new OpenStax reading during the transfer assessment. Use only the references permitted in the assessment plan; revisit a focused section after feedback.

TEACHER NOTES

Two-meeting assessment: This is the first of two full class periods. Day 13 is for completion, peer defense, final revision, and submission. The preceding synthesis lesson is retained.

Assessment conventions: Use the Unit 1 rubric: Science / Reasoning / Communication / Transfer-to-Asteroid. Score the four dimensions independently from 0–4; report the profile without averaging and use the established lowest-dimension conversion. Science checks the physics; Reasoning checks the choice and justification of the model; Communication checks labeled, organized work; Transfer-to-Asteroid checks the supported connection and its limits. Peer and student ratings are feedback; the teacher makes the final judgment. Target self-ratings use the separate 1–3 scale and do not automatically become mastery ratings. Revisions follow Unit 1’s two-week window, with new evidence for a one-level move on a dimension.

CPA access: Supply agreed labeled diagrams or vector components when component derivation is not the assessed target. Keep the same physics prompt and rubric; Honors students can justify or derive the corresponding model.

Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.
